data.title: Certificate Transparency Discloses Internal Naming
data.summary: Every certificate issued for the organisation's domains is published in public logs, disclosing hostnames that were never meant to be found — development, staging, administrative and pre-release systems among them.
data.description:
Certificate transparency exists so that mis-issued certificates can be detected, and it works by publishing every certificate to append-only public logs. The practical consequence is that issuing a certificate publishes the hostname.

Teams routinely request certificates for internal names on the assumption that an unpublished DNS record keeps a host private. It does not: the name appears in the logs within minutes, and tooling watches those logs continuously.

The names themselves are informative beyond their existence. `vpn-test`, `jenkins`, `backup-admin` and `sap-dev` tell an attacker what the estate runs and which hosts are least likely to be monitored.
data.recommendation:
* Treat any name in a certificate as public, and name hosts accordingly.
* Use a wildcard certificate for internal hosts where the risk model allows, so individual names are not published.
* Keep genuinely internal services on an internal certificate authority that does not log publicly.
* Monitor the logs for your own domains, both to find forgotten assets and to detect mis-issuance.
data.short_recommendation: Use wildcards for internal names, and expect everything else to be public.
